corpus_gaps: No provision in the frozen corpus governs the creation, reservation or determination of a life interest reserved by a donor on a notarial deed of gift. That the donee's ownership is burdened during the donor's life and falls in free on the donor's death is Roman-Dutch common law, to which s 36 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance itself defers. Step 2 of the devolution chain therefore cannot be supported from statute alone.

No corpus provision states the general-law rule that a building erected on land accedes to the land, so the passing of the commercial building bearing Assessment No. 12 with Lot A under Deed of Gift No. 1012 rests on common law. s 3 of the Ordinance only makes things attached to the earth 'immovable property' for the purposes of that Ordinance; it does not decide ownership of the building.

No corpus provision fixes the validity or the irrevocability of a deed of gift as between donor and donee. Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s 2 (7-1840/s2) on its face covers sale, purchase, transfer, assignment and mortgage, and the corpus text of that section carries amendment events dated 2022 and 2024, after the matter reference date; it was therefore not relied on.

The Ordinance does not resolve how the collateral half under s 25 (one parent surviving) divides between full-blood siblings and half-blood siblings on the deceased parent's side. s 27 states a full-blood preference but is placed after s 26, which governs the different case of both parents failing, while s 30 directs a per capita division 'except when otherwise expressly provided'. Choosing between them needs judicial authority outside this corpus.

Whether the parties are governed by the general law rather than Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai (s 2 of the Ordinance) is not stated in the scenario and cannot be established from the corpus. Nor does the scenario say whether Minoli was living at each relevant death, or whether Nishantha's earlier marriage ended by death or by divorce.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the governing law for intestate succession to Lot A. Lot A with the commercial building on it is immovable property in Sri Lanka, so the 2009 and 2010 intestacies are regulated by Part III of this Ordinance.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; the corpus records no amendment event on this section, so the text stood unchanged at each of the three deaths (2007, 2009, 2010) and at 2021-10.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
provisions.why_relevant: Lalantha died intestate on 04.10.2009 leaving his wife Nishi Fernando surviving, so Nishi takes one half of Lot A before any question of descendants, ascendants or collaterals arises. Harsha died unmarried, so the section is not engaged on his death.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the text applied at Lalantha's death in 2009 and at 2021-10.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
provisions.why_relevant: Sets the order in which the residue after the spouse's half is taken and makes clear that the spouse's half under s 22 comes off first. It is the hinge between s 22 and ss 24 to 25 for Lalantha's estate.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.
provisions.why_relevant: Explains why no descendant takes on either intestacy: Lalantha and Harsha both died issueless, so the descendant class fails and the inheritance moves on to ascendants and collaterals. It also explains why Ashen and Tashen take nothing while their mother Dushani is living, representation running only through a deceased child.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half, and the brothers and sisters of the deceased of the full blood, and the issue of any deceased brother or sister of the full blood, by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, and the issue of any such deceased brother or sister of the half-blood, by representation, take the other half.
provisions.why_relevant: The operative rule for both deaths. On each of Lalantha's and Harsha's death the descendants failed, the father Nishantha had predeceased (13.09.2007) and the mother Kanthi survived. Kanthi therefore takes half of the estate then in question and the other half goes to the full-blood siblings together with the half-blood sister Minoli, who is related through the deceased parent.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus, so the text applied in 2009, in 2010 and at 2021-10.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: but if there are only half-brothers and sisters or such issue of one side, the full brothers and sisters and the issue of deceased full brothers and sisters by representation, take then in the first place one-half of the property, and divide the other half with the half-brothers and sisters and their issue by representation.
provisions.why_relevant: Recorded because it is the competing reading of how the collateral half splits between the full-blood siblings and Minoli. If s 27 reaches the s 25 collateral half, the full-blood siblings take a preference and the arithmetic changes. The section sits after s 26, which deals with both parents failing, so its reach into the s 25 one-surviving-parent case is open. This is the main reason the shares question cannot be closed on statute alone.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Except when otherwise expressly provided, if all those who succeed to the inheritance are equally near in degree to the intestate, they take per capita, and not per stirpes.
provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the division inside the collateral half under s 25. Harsha, Dushani and Minoli are all siblings of Lalantha and so equally near in degree; on the reading taken here they share that half per capita. The words 'except when otherwise expressly provided' are what leave room for the s 27 argument.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: In all questions relating to the distribution of the property of an intestate, if the present Ordinance is silent, the rules of the Roman-Dutch law as it prevailed in North Holland are to govern and be followed.
provisions.why_relevant: The Ordinance itself refers questions it does not answer to Roman-Dutch law. It is the statutory hook for the two non-statutory steps this matter needs, the effect of the life interest reserved on Deed of Gift No. 1012 and the division of the collateral half where the Ordinance is silent. Its presence is why both questions are classified as mixed rather than statute only.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1876; no amendment event recorded in the corpus.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: includes land, incorporeal tenements, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth, and any interest in land except that of a mortgagee

The excerpt is the definition of 'immovable property'; the corpus body of s 3 has lost the defined-term labels, which the verifier should confirm against the source text.

The scenario says nothing about the personal law of the Jayakodi family, so the answer proceeds on the unstated assumption that they are governed by the general law and not by Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The intestate links in the chain, Lalantha's death in 2009 and Harsha's death in 2010, are governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance and can be sourced from the corpus. The first link cannot. Title moved from Nishantha to Lalantha by Deed of Gift No. 1012 subject to a reserved life interest, and the pedigree only reaches Lalantha as absolute owner once that life interest determines on the donor's death in 2007. Nothing in the frozen corpus governs the reservation or determination of a life interest, or the accession of the commercial building to the land; s 36 of the Ordinance sends those questions to Roman-Dutch law, which is outside the corpus.

enrichment.original_background: Nishantha Jayakodi was allotted by the final decree of Partition case bearing No.102/P dated 25.03.2002 in the District Court of Colombo, the allotment of land marked Lot containing in extent 20 perches depicted in Partition Plan No. 808 dated 08.01.2001 made by K. N. A. Perera Licensed Surveyor. He built a commercial building on this land bearing Assessment No.12, Arunodaya Mawatha, Battaramulla. Nishantha Jayakodi upon Deed of Gift No.1012 dated 12.08.2002 attested by S. Kumarasiri Notary Public of Colombo gifted the said Lot A depicted in the said Plan No. 808 unto his youngest son Lalantha Jayakodi subject to the life interest of the donor as a gift absolute and irrevocable. Nishantha Jayakodi died intestate on 13.09.2007 leaving as his heirs his wife Kanthi and his three children Lalantha, Harsha and Dushani. Nishantha was previously married and had a child namely Minoli. His youngest son Lalantha was married to Nishi Fernando. Lalantha died on 04.10.2009 intestate and issueless. Dushani was married to Sarath and had two children namely Ashen and Tashen. Harsha I was unmarried and issueless, Harsha died intestate on 18.05.2010. 2. On the death of Lalantha Jayakodi, Kanthi filed the Testamentary Case bearing No.4620/T in District Court of Colombo to administer the estate of her late son. The Letters of Administration dated 26.12.2009 were issued to her and the proceedings were terminated on 26.04.2010.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question asks for the pedigree, that is the chain by which title to Lot A in Plan No. 808 together with the commercial building bearing Assessment No. 12 moved from Nishantha Jayakodi to the persons who own it today. Four transmissions have to be traced: the partition decree of 25.03.2002, the deed of gift of 12.08.2002 with the life interest reserved to the donor, the intestacy of Lalantha on 04.10.2009, and the intestacy of Harsha on 18.05.2010.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876, s.21(1), and 'immovable property' under s.3 of that Ordinance includes land and things attached to the earth, so Lot A and the building on it are covered. Part III applies to the estate of any person dying after the proclamation of the Ordinance, s.20, and does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai, s.2. Where an intestate leaves a surviving spouse, the spouse inherits one half, s.22, and the residue devolves in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals, s.23. Descendants are preferent and the issue of a deceased child take by representation, s.24. Where the descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half of the residue and the other half goes to the full-blood brothers and sisters together with the half-blood brothers and sisters related to the intestate through the deceased parent, s.25. Persons equally near in degree take per capita and not per stirpes unless the Ordinance expressly provides otherwise, s.30. Where the Ordinance is silent the rules of Roman-Dutch law govern, s.36. The Ordinance does not itself govern the effect of a life interest reserved by a donor on a deed of gift.
gold_answer_draft.application: By the final decree of 25.03.2002 in DC Colombo case 102/P, Nishantha Jayakodi became sole owner of Lot A, and the commercial building he erected on the land forms part of that immovable property, s.3. By Deed of Gift No. 1012 dated 12.08.2002 he gifted Lot A to his youngest son Lalantha absolutely and irrevocably, reserving a life interest to himself, so that from that date Lalantha held the ownership burdened by the donor's life interest. On the donor's death on 13.09.2007 the life interest determined and Lalantha held Lot A free of it. Nishantha's own intestacy of 2007 does not touch this land, because he had already parted with the ownership in 2002 and retained only a life interest that ended with him, so his widow Kanthi and his children take nothing in Lot A through his estate. Lalantha died intestate and issueless on 04.10.2009 leaving his wife Nishi Fernando, his mother Kanthi, his full brother Harsha, his full sister Dushani and his half-sister Minoli through his father. Nishi takes one half under s.22. The residue of one half devolves under s.23, and since Lalantha left no descendants s.24 is exhausted, so s.25 applies: his father had predeceased him and his mother survived, so Kanthi takes half of that residue, a quarter of the whole, and the other quarter goes to Harsha and Dushani as full-blood siblings together with Minoli, a half-blood sister related through the deceased father. Those three are equally near in degree and, on the reading taken here, share that quarter per capita under s.30, one twelfth each. The letters of administration issued to Kanthi in testamentary case 4620/T on 26.12.2009 and terminated on 26.04.2010 are the machinery by which Lalantha's estate was administered; they do not alter the devolution worked out above. Harsha then died intestate, unmarried and issueless on 18.05.2010 holding one twelfth. There is no spouse and no descendant, so s.25 applies again: his mother Kanthi takes half of that one twelfth and the other half goes to his full sister Dushani together with Minoli, in equal parts under s.30, Lalantha having predeceased him without issue to represent him. Ashen and Tashen take nothing at any stage, because their mother Dushani is living and representation under s.24 operates only through a deceased child.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Subject to the matters this corpus cannot settle, the pedigree runs: Nishantha Jayakodi, sole owner from the final decree of 25.03.2002; to Lalantha Jayakodi by Deed of Gift No. 1012 of 12.08.2002, subject to the donor's life interest; that life interest ending with Nishantha's death on 13.09.2007, leaving Lalantha absolute owner; on Lalantha's intestate death on 04.10.2009 to his widow Nishi Fernando, his mother Kanthi and his siblings Harsha, Dushani and Minoli; and on Harsha's intestate death on 18.05.2010 his share passing to his mother Kanthi, his sister Dushani and his half-sister Minoli. The present owners are therefore Nishi Fernando, Kanthi, Dushani and Minoli. Two links cannot be closed from the statutory corpus alone: the effect of the reserved life interest and the passing of the building with the land are Roman-Dutch questions referred out by s.36, and the split of the collateral half between full-blood and half-blood siblings depends on whether s.27 or s.30 governs. The pedigree is also stated on assumptions the facts do not supply, that the family is governed by the general law, s.2, and that Minoli was living at each relevant death.

answer_claims.claim_text: Intestate succession to Lot A and the commercial building on it is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, because they are immovable property in Sri Lanka and each death occurred long after the proclamation of the Ordinance.

Part III does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai, so the pedigree rests on the assumption that the Jayakodi family is governed by the general law.
Where an intestate leaves a surviving spouse the spouse inherits one half of the property, and only the residue passes through the order of descendants, ascendants and collaterals.

Where the descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half of the residue and the other half goes to the full-blood siblings together with the half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent.
Persons equally near in degree to the intestate take per capita and not per stirpes, except where the Ordinance expressly provides otherwise.
The issue of a deceased child take by representation, so Ashen and Tashen take nothing while their mother Dushani is living.

Lalantha held Lot A subject to his father's reserved life interest from 12.08.2002 and held it free of that burden from 13.09.2007; this step rests on Roman-Dutch law, to which the Ordinance defers where it is silent, and no provision in this corpus supports it.
Nishantha's intestacy of 13.09.2007 adds no link to the chain of title to Lot A, because he had already conveyed the ownership in 2002 and retained only a life interest that ended at his death.
On Lalantha's intestate death on 04.10.2009 his widow Nishi Fernando took one half, his surviving mother Kanthi took one quarter, and the remaining quarter went to Harsha, Dushani and Minoli.
On Harsha's intestate death on 18.05.2010, unmarried and issueless, his share passed half to his surviving mother Kanthi and half to his sister Dushani and his half-sister Minoli.
The letters of administration issued to Kanthi in testamentary case 4620/T are administration machinery and do not change the devolution of Lot A.

The pedigree runs from Nishantha to Lalantha by deed of gift, then on Lalantha's intestacy to Nishi Fernando, Kanthi, Harsha, Dushani and Minoli, and then on Harsha's intestacy to Kanthi, Dushani and Minoli, leaving Nishi Fernando, Kanthi, Dushani and Minoli as the present owners.

questions.block_reason: The devolution chain has a link that no provision in the frozen corpus supports. Whether the reserved life interest left Lalantha with the ownership from 12.08.2002 and freed it on the donor's death, and whether the commercial building passed with the land, are Roman-Dutch questions that s 36 of the Ordinance refers outside this Ordinance and outside this corpus. The statutory links from Lalantha's and Harsha's intestacies are set out and can be verified, but the pedigree as a whole is not statute only. Two further open points, the personal law of the family under s 2 and whether Minoli was living at each relevant death, are recorded as assumptions rather than findings.

Choosing between them changes each share and needs judicial authority outside the corpus.

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question is what fraction of Lot A, with the commercial building bearing Assessment No. 12, each surviving heir holds at the reference date. That requires the whole to be divided twice, first on Lalantha's intestate death on 04.10.2009 and again on Harsha's intestate death on 18.05.2010.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance governs intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka, s.21(1), and 'immovable property' under s.3 covers land and things attached to the earth. A surviving spouse inherits one half, s.22, and the residue devolves as respects descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals, s.23. Descendants are preferent and the issue of a deceased child take by representation, s.24. Where descendants fail and one parent survives, that parent takes half the residue and the other half goes to the full-blood siblings and to the half-blood siblings related through the deceased parent, s.25. Those equally near in degree take per capita unless the Ordinance expressly provides otherwise, s.30, while s.27 states a full-blood preference in the case of half-brothers and sisters. Where the Ordinance is silent, Roman-Dutch law governs, s.36.
gold_answer_draft.application: Taking Lalantha as absolute owner of the whole on 04.10.2009, which depends on the reserved life interest having ended with the donor in 2007, his widow Nishi Fernando takes one half under s.22. He left no descendants, so under s.23 and s.24 the residue of one half moves past the descendant class to s.25. His father Nishantha had predeceased him and his mother Kanthi survived, so Kanthi takes half of that residue, a one quarter share of the whole, and the remaining one quarter goes to his full brother Harsha, his full sister Dushani and his half-sister Minoli, who is related to him through the deceased father. All three are siblings and equally near in degree, so on the per capita division under s.30 each takes one twelfth of the whole. Harsha then died intestate, unmarried and issueless on 18.05.2010 holding one twelfth. He left no spouse and no descendant, his father was dead and his mother Kanthi alive, so s.25 applies again: Kanthi takes half of the one twelfth, that is one twenty fourth, and the other one twenty fourth goes to Dushani and Minoli in equal parts under s.30, one forty eighth each, Lalantha having predeceased without issue to be represented. Adding the two rounds, Kanthi holds one quarter plus one twenty fourth, and Dushani and Minoli each hold one twelfth plus one forty eighth. Ashen and Tashen hold nothing, because representation under s.24 runs only through a deceased child and their mother Dushani is living. If instead the full-blood preference in s.27 is carried into the s.25 collateral half, the sibling shares change and Minoli takes materially less than Harsha and Dushani, so the figures given are not the only reading the Ordinance will bear.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: On the per capita reading of s.30, the shares held at the reference date are: Nishi Fernando one half; Kanthi seven twenty fourths, that is fourteen forty eighths; Dushani five forty eighths; and Minoli five forty eighths. Those add to the whole. Ashen and Tashen hold nothing. The figures are proposed, not settled. They depend on Lalantha having owned the whole at his death, which turns on the Roman-Dutch effect of the reserved life interest that s.36 refers outside the Ordinance, and on the s.30 per capita division prevailing over the full-blood preference in s.27. They also assume the family is governed by the general law under s.2 and that Minoli and Kanthi were living at each relevant date.

answer_claims.claim_text: Part III of the Ordinance governs the division of Lot A and the building on it, since they are immovable property in Sri Lanka and every death fell after the proclamation of the Ordinance.
A surviving spouse inherits one half of the intestate's property, and only the residue passes through the descendant, ascendant and collateral order.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half of the residue and the full-blood siblings together with the half-blood siblings on the deceased parent's side take the other half.
Heirs equally near in degree take per capita unless the Ordinance expressly provides otherwise, and s.27 states a competing full-blood preference in the case of half-brothers and sisters.
Nishi Fernando takes one half of Lot A as Lalantha's surviving spouse.
Kanthi takes one quarter of Lot A out of Lalantha's estate as the surviving parent, his father having predeceased him and his descendants having failed.
The remaining quarter of Lalantha's estate is taken by Harsha, Dushani and Minoli in equal one twelfth shares, Minoli qualifying as a half-blood sister related through the deceased father.
Harsha's one twelfth passes on his death half to Kanthi as surviving parent, that is one twenty fourth, and the other half to Dushani and Minoli in equal one forty eighth shares.
Ashen and Tashen hold no share, because representation operates only through a deceased child and their mother Dushani is living.

The starting point that Lalantha owned the whole of Lot A on 04.10.2009 rests on the Roman-Dutch effect of the reserved life interest, which the Ordinance refers outside itself and which no corpus provision supplies.
On the per capita reading the present shares are Nishi Fernando one half, Kanthi seven twenty fourths, Dushani five forty eighths and Minoli five forty eighths, which together make the whole.
Those fractions are not the only division the Ordinance will bear, because a full-blood preference under s.27 applied to the collateral half would reduce Minoli's share and raise Dushani's.

questions.block_reason: Two things stop this from being a statute only answer. The whole calculation begins from Lalantha owning the entirety of Lot A on 04.10.2009, which depends on the Roman-Dutch effect of the life interest reserved on Deed of Gift No. 1012 and on the building acceding to the land, neither of which any corpus provision governs and both of which s 36 of the Ordinance refers to Roman-Dutch law. Separately, the Ordinance does not settle whether the collateral half under s 25 divides per capita under s 30 or with a full-blood preference under s 27, and the two readings give different fractions to Dushani and Minoli. The fractions stated are the per capita reading and are offered for the verifier and the lawyer to test, not as a settled result.
